name: Mastopexy

image.caption: 10614 Dr. Placik Breast Lift Chicago, Illinois Arlington Heights

lead: Mastopexy is a plastic surgery procedure that lifts sagging breasts by removing excess skin, tightening supporting tissue and repositioning the nipple-areola complex higher on the breast. It is used after pregnancy, weight loss, menopause or implant removal, and can be combined with implants or breast reduction.

The appearance payoff is a higher, firmer-looking breast shape. Surgeons choose an incision pattern from the degree of sagging, and a 2024 randomised trial examined a modified periareolar approach with fat grafting in complex ptosis.

paras: The surgeon grades the sagging (the Regnault scale runs from I to IV), then selects a technique: periareolar (around the areola), vertical or lollipop, or anchor (inverted-T) incisions, or the Regnault B technique. Support tape and a supportive bra are used during recovery, and scars mature over about a year.

Common effects include bleeding, infection and temporary numbness. Serious ones include seroma, haematoma, wound breakdown, and skin or nipple necrosis, more likely with smoking, diabetes and obesity. Scars can be long-lasting and asymmetry may persist. A 2013 review says combined augmentation and mastopexy carries the greatest complication potential and that mastopexy has the highest incidence of litigation among aesthetic breast procedures.

web.title: Europe PMC records for four mastopexy-related papers

chain: Excess skin removed and tissue supported
angle.text: The operation reshapes the skin envelope and repositions the nipple-areola complex so the breast sits higher on the chest. People use it to restore a lifted contour after volume loss or stretching.

lead: Mastopexy, commonly called a breast lift, is a plastic surgery operation that raises sagging breasts by removing excess skin, reshaping and supporting the breast tissue and moving the nipple-areola complex to a higher position.[1] People choose it for a higher, firmer-looking breast contour after pregnancy, weight loss, menopause or implant removal, and it can be combined with implants or a breast reduction.[1][2]

Surgeons grade the amount of sagging with the modified Regnault scale, which runs from I (mild) to IV (severe) according to where the nipple sits relative to the fold under the breast, and then choose an incision pattern: around the areola, vertical, or anchor-shaped.[1] Support tape and a surgical bra are used in recovery, and scars take about a year to mature.[1]

Research on mastopexy consists mainly of surgical reviews and case series, with a small number of randomized trials of technique variants.[3][4][2] A 2013 review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery describes evaluation, incision options and implant placement, and notes that combined augmentation and mastopexy carries the greatest complication potential.[3][2]
infobox: Modified Regnault scale, I to IV[1]
Tape removed at 7 to 10 days; scars mature over about a year[1]

paras: Wikipedia lists sagging after pregnancy, weight loss or menopause, after breast implant removal, congenital or tuberous breast deformity, post-mastectomy reconstruction, and pseudoptosis, where the lower breast sags while the nipple stays high[1].

Wikipedia identifies gravity as the most common cause of breast ptosis, with contributing factors including volume loss after pregnancy and lactation, menopause and skin inelasticity.[1] Surgeons grade ptosis by the position of the nipple relative to the inframammary fold on the modified Regnault scale, I (mild) to IV (severe); Wikipedia also mentions an alternative classification published by Laurence Anthony Kirwan, said to suit surgical planning better, and describes pseudoptosis, in which the lower breast hangs while the nipple stays at or above the fold.[1]

A review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery lists the elements surgeons assess before choosing a technique: the patient's goals, degree of ptosis, tissue volume, skin quality and breast position.[3][2]

Anchor (inverted-T) lifts use three incisions and allow the largest corrections but leave the most scars. Periareolar lifts use an incision around the areola for milder ptosis. Vertical (lollipop) lifts add a vertical incision, and the Regnault B technique uses a curvilinear incision that avoids the medial vertical scar. Pedicle choice (superior, inferior or medial) maintains blood supply to the nipple-areola complex[1]. Other reviews describe vertical and SPAIR mammaplasty techniques for reduction and lift[5][6].

Mastopexy can be combined with implants as augmentation-mastopexy. Wikipedia notes that combining the two procedures carries higher complication and revision rates than either alone[1], and a 2013 review states the same[3].

Wikipedia also describes a circumareolar (donut) lift for milder cases, which removes a ring of skin around the areola, and a crescent lift above the areola for mild ptosis; the anchor pattern is used for severe ptosis, and its fold scar is the most prone to thickening.[1] Surgeons also describe the preservation of the nipple-areola complex's blood supply and sensation as the key technical concern.[1]
Wikipedia describes support tape removed at 7 to 10 days, a supportive bra afterwards, weekly visits in the first three weeks and final contour taking about a year as scars mature[1].

Common effects are bleeding, infection, anaesthesia effects and temporary numbness; serious ones are seroma, haematoma, wound breakdown and skin or nipple necrosis, with smoking, aspirin use, diabetes and obesity linked to higher necrosis rates. Scars may be visible long term and can affect self-examination and mammograms[1]. A 2013 review notes mastopexy has the greatest incidence of litigation among aesthetic breast procedures[3].

Numbness or tingling is common after surgery and usually improves, while permanent numbness is described as rare.[1] Surgeons aim to preserve nipple-areola viability because it bears on sensation and on breastfeeding; Wikipedia does not give frequency data for effects on breastfeeding.[1] Scars can complicate breast self-examination and mammograms, although benign changes are usually distinguishable from cancer, and Wikipedia says women at high breast cancer risk may need an individualized discussion.[1]

A 2024 randomized open-label trial in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery compared a modified peri-areolar mastopexy with implants and fat grafting (40 women) against traditional peri-areolar mastopexy with implants (35 women), all with moderate to severe ptosis. At 12 months, 75 percent of the study group (30 women) reported excellent results versus 60 percent of controls (21); the study group also showed a greater vertical nipple-areola shift and higher satisfaction, and the authors concluded the technique was safe and effective.[4][2]

A 2016 letter indexed as a randomized trial examined full-thickness periareolar skin resection in mastopexy.[7][2] A 2007 retrospective study cited on Wikipedia followed 40 women who had the Regnault B technique (13 lifts and 27 with augmentation) and reported no medical complications, one scar revision and satisfaction in all patients.[1]

Population-scale data come from the International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery's global surveys: a 14-year analysis reported about 34.9 million aesthetic procedures in 2023, of which breast lift appeared in the surgical top five in 2022.[8][2]

timeline.event: A review of the SPAIR mammaplasty, a reduction and lift technique, is published in Clinics in Plastic Surgery.[6]
A review of vertical reduction mammaplasty is published in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery.[5]
A retrospective study of 40 women treated with the Regnault B technique reports satisfaction in all patients.[1]
Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery publishes a review of mastopexy noting the highest litigation incidence among aesthetic breast procedures.[3]
A letter on full-thickness periareolar skin resection in mastopexy is published.[7]
Breast lift temporarily enters the ISAPS global top five surgical procedures.[2]
A randomized trial of modified periareolar mastopexy with fat grafting is published.[4]
